### Observed differences

- All qualifying differences lie in resource allocation: the resource family produced 7 evidence items from 10 tested units, where fewer than 0.01 items would be expected by chance, while control flow (0 items; 0.17 expected) and timing (0 items; 0.014 expected) produced none. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- In the later window, six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22) show a shared reallocation pattern. User_104's share of assignments fell to roughly half its earlier level (A22: about 20 in 100 to about 8; A01: about 13 to about 7; A17: about 11 to about 5), User_67's share rose on all six (A17: about 9 to 14; A13/A14: about 8 to 13), and User_77, not among the leading shares before, took about 5–8 in 100 afterwards. Several other previously leading resources dropped out of the top shares while previously minor ones gained, and the share spread over many minor resources ("OTHER") grew from roughly 27–42 in 100 to 34–49 in 100. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- A07 shows a near-complete turnover instead: of the ten resources leading its assignment shares in the earlier window, only three remain among the leading ten in the later window, and the new leading resources — each with little or no share before — took roughly 5–9 in 100 each. [ASSIGN003]
- The profiles rest on similar observation volumes in both windows (for example 200 vs 200 for A01, 257 vs 280 for A13/A14, 127 vs 118 for A22), and each item's difference exceeded about 999.5 in 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data. A13 and A14 have identical profiles, so they most likely reflect one underlying allocation behaviour rather than two independent confirmations. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that resource allocation changed across seven activities. On A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, assignment shares moved from one group of resources to another: User_104's share roughly halved, User_67's share grew on every one of them, and User_77 took a regular share after being absent from the leading shares; on A07, assignments shifted almost entirely to a different set of resources. Supporting signs: the resource family yielded 7 qualifying items against fewer than 0.01 expected without change, all items agree in direction on every resource they share, the profiles rest on 118–280 observations per window, and no control-flow or timing item qualified, so the difference appears confined to allocation rather than to structure or timing. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

Limitations: A13 and A14 show identical profiles and are not independent confirmations; the per-activity shares cannot show whether the rising and falling resources exchanged work on the same cases; and a changed mix of cases reaching these activities, rather than a change in allocation itself, cannot be ruled out, although the absence of qualifying control-flow differences argues against it. [ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005]

Let me analyse this evidence.

Schema: pcr-evidence-2.1. Windows: 200 before, 200 after traces.

Screening: 73 units tested, 0.19 items expected without change overall. By family:
- control_flow: 35 units tested, 0 items, 0.17 expected
- time: 28 units tested, 0 items, 0.014 expected
- resources: 10 units tested, 7 items, 0.005 expected

Evidence: 7 ASSIGN items (O_ASSIGN indicator) for activities A01, A03, A07, A13, A14, A17, A22. All show cosine dissimilarity ~0.33–0.39, empirical_strength 0.9995 (i.e., larger than 99.95% of reference comparisons). All characterized as "redistributed".

The resource family: 7 items observed vs 0.005 expected without change. That's 1400× the expectation. Per the instructions: "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole, even when all items describe one underlying difference; do not merge items for this comparison." So the resource family count (7 vs 0.005) is many times larger — this passes the screening comparison. Control flow: 0 items vs 0.17 expected — nothing. Time: 0 items vs 0.014 expected — nothing.

So we have a resource allocation change hypothesis. The evidence contains resource items (ASSIGN), so we can discuss resources. No TWAIT items, no CONC/HAND items — only ASSIGN. So we discuss allocation changes.

Now let's look at the patterns:

ASSIGN001 (A01): Before top: User_104 (0.13), User_16 (0.08), User_67 (0.08), User_58, User_66... After: User_67 (0.125), User_104 (0.065), User_77 (0.065), User_5, User_51... So User_104 halved (13% → 6.5%), User_16 disappeared from top (8% → below), User_67 rose (8% → 12.5%), User_77 appeared (0 → 6.5%). OTHER rose from 38% to 44.5%.

ASSIGN002 (A03): similar pattern. User_104 12.6% → 6%, User_16 7% → out, User_67 8.5% → 12.6%, User_77 0 → 6%, User_51 0 → 5%. OTHER 39% → 47%.

ASSIGN003 (A07): completely different set of users. Before: User_109, User_29, User_87 (~10% each), User_100, User_30, User_75, User_68, User_123, User_99, User_121. After: User_123 (9.2%), User_113 (8.5%), User_131 (7.8%), User_68 (7.8%), User_133 (7.1%), User_83, User_112, User_122, User_100, User_120. So a wholesale replacement of the workforce on A07: User_109, User_29, User_87, User_30, User_75, User_99, User_121 all dropped out of top; new users User_113, User_131, User_133, User_83, User_112, User_122, User_120 appeared. Only User_100, User_68, User_123 persist. Support: 163 before, 141 after.

ASSIGN004 (A13) and ASSIGN005 (A14): identical profiles (same components before and after, same support 257/280). Interesting — A13 and A14 have identical assignment profiles. Before: User_104 10.5%, User_67 8.2%, User_16 7%, User_58 5.8%... After: User_67 13.2%, User_77 5.4%, User_40 5%, User_104 4.6%... Same pattern as A01/A03: User_104 halved, User_16 gone, User_67 up, User_77 new.

ASSIGN006 (A17): same pattern. User_104 11.3% → 5.1%, User_16 7.1% → out, User_67 8.8% → 14%, User_77 0 → 5.1%, User_40, User_51 new. OTHER 40% → 47.5%.

ASSIGN007 (A22): User_104 19.7% → 8.5% (biggest drop), User_67 13.4% → 17.8%, User_77 0 → 7.6%, User_51, User_52 up, User_66 down 8.7% → 5.1%. OTHER 26.8% → 33.9%.

So the consistent pattern across six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22): work shifts away from a group including User_104, User_16, User_58, User_66, User_4, User_61, User_48, User_42 toward a group including User_67, User_77, User_40, User_51, User_5, User_14, User_2, User_52. User_67 gains share everywhere. User_104 loses share everywhere (roughly halving). User_77 appears from nothing to ~5–8%. A07 shows a complete turnover of its performer pool.

Constraint: "name at most three codes in the whole answer". So I can name at most three resource codes total. I'll pick User_104, User_67, User_77 as the three most illustrative. I must be careful not to name others. I can describe groups without naming: "a set of previously frequent resources", "several resources not previously among the top assignees".

Also: "do not infer roles, people or teams". So describe as "resources" / "allocation", not "staff left" or "team reorganisation".

Now the judgement:

Screening comparison per family: resources 7 items vs 0.005 expected — many orders of magnitude larger. This is not what an unchanged process produces. So we go beyond "insufficient evidence" on the count test.

Then judge by directness, consistency, ability to rule out competing explanations.

The hypothesis: resource allocation for these activities changed — assignments redistributed from one set of resources to another. This is directly shown by ASSIGN items (O_ASSIGN profiles). All seven items agree in direction for the shared resources: User_104 down in all six (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22), User_67 up in all six, User_77 up (from unobserved) in all six. A07 shows a full replacement of its pool. Consistency is high.

Competing explanations: Could this be sampling variation? The empirical strength 0.9995 for each item says each individual difference is unusual for random re-splits. And the count comparison (7 vs 0.005) already rules out chance at the family level. Could it be a rare-variant artifact? These are not rare variants — support is high (127–280 observations per window). Could the change be something else, e.g., a change in how often activities occur? No — the profiles are conditional on the activity occurring; support counts show activities still occur at similar rates (A01: 200/200 both; A03: 199/199; A07: 163→141; A13/A14: 257→280; A17: 238→257; A22: 127→118). Participation roughly stable; the composition of assignees changed.

What can't be ruled out: whether this reflects a deliberate reallocation vs. e.g. a shift in case mix — but we shouldn't speculate about causes. The competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out: we only see assignment shares for activities that occurred; we cannot tell whether the same underlying pool change affected unobserved activities, and we cannot distinguish a reallocation of work from changes driven by which cases entered the windows... Hmm, actually the instruction says "Briefly mention an important competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out." For resource items, a competing explanation could be that the observed redistribution stems from changes in the case mix routed to these activities rather than a change in allocation policy — but that's speculative. Better: the evidence shows correlation across activities but cannot show whether the newly appearing resources took over from the declining ones on the same cases (no HAND/CONC items to show handovers or concentration directly). Also, since only ASSIGN items qualified, we cannot tell whether the redistribution changed overall workload concentration (CONC) — no such items.

Actually, a cleaner competing explanation: the profiles are over assignment shares; a change in the volume mix of cases (different case types routed differently) could produce shifted assignee shares without any reallocation rule change. The evidence cannot rule that out because there is no control-flow or timing evidence qualifying. Hmm, but I shouldn't over-speculate. Let me phrase: "The evidence cannot show whether the declining and rising resources exchanged work on the same cases, nor whether the shift stems from a reallocation or from a changed mix of cases reaching these activities."

Support level: Supported hypothesis? Let's check criteria: "Supported hypothesis: the evidence supports a specific hypothesis directly and consistently." The ASSIGN indicator directly measures allocation. Seven items, all consistent, family count 7 vs 0.005 expected — cannot be chance. Directness: ASSIGN is the direct indicator for allocation. Consistency: same direction across six activities; A07 is a different flavour (full turnover) but still a redistribution. I think "Supported hypothesis" is right.

Wait — one caution: ASSIGN004 and ASSIGN005 are identical (A13 and A14 have identical profiles and supports). That suggests they may be the same underlying behaviour counted twice, or the two activities share the same assignee pool. The instruction says "Several indicators and activities can reflect the same trace behaviour; agreeing items are not automatically independent confirmations." So I should note that A13 and A14 show identical profiles and may reflect one shared allocation change, and that items are not independent confirmations. But even discounting duplicates, we have 6 distinct activities with consistent shifts, and the family-level count comparison (7 vs 0.005) stands.

Hypothesis statement: "In the later window, assignment work for a set of activities (A01, A03, A07, A13, A14, A17, A22) was redistributed across resources: shares moved away from a group of previously dominant resources toward a different group, with User_104's share roughly halving on six activities and User_67's share rising on the same six, while User_77 — absent from the top shares before — took about 5–8% of assignments after; on A07 the performer pool turned over almost completely."

But "name at most three codes in the whole answer" — so User_104, User_67, User_77 are my three. I must not name User_16, User_58, etc. I'll describe them as "several other previously frequent resources" and "several resources previously little or not involved".

1. Resource family: 7 of 10 tested resource units qualified vs fewer than 0.01 expected by chance; control flow (0 of 35 vs 0.17 expected) and time (0 of 28 vs 0.014 expected) produced nothing. So the differences are confined to resource allocation.
